passage: Bhavna, you'll laugh. My neighbour, Kusum Aunty, first asked me to water her tulsi while she was away. Easy, yes. Then to feed her cat. Fine. Then to let the plumber in. Okay. Yesterday she called: "Beta, since you're already doing so much, could you stay at my flat for the week? The house shouldn't be empty." I opened my mouth to say yes. It felt so natural, like the next stair. And then I asked myself: Minakshi, if she had asked this on day one, would you have agreed? No way. I have my own flat, my own work. So I told her, "Aunty, I'm happy to keep watering and feeding, but I can't stay over." She said, "Oh, of course." That was it. I'd built it into a huge thing in my head.

qa.a: That the watering and feeding would continue but staying over wasn't possible; it kept the fair help while refusing the step Minakshi would never have agreed to at first.

Monday: Kishore, secretary of the residents' association in their Vadodara building, knocked on Ujjwal's door. 'Can you collect this month's maintenance from your floor? Just six flats.' Easy. Ujjwal said yes.
Two weeks later: 'You did it so well. Could you also do floors three and four? Same thing.' Ujjwal hesitated, then agreed.
A month later: Kishore came with a thick file. 'Since you're already handling so much, would you be treasurer for the year? The accounts, the audit, all of it.' Ujjwal's mouth was already opening to say yes. It felt like the obvious next step. He stopped. 'Give me till tomorrow.' That night he asked himself one question: if Kishore had knocked on day one and asked him to be treasurer, would he have said yes? No. Not with his night shifts. The next morning he said, 'I'll keep collecting from my floor. But I can't be treasurer.' Kishore sighed, then nodded.

qa.a: He felt tempted to agree because it seemed the obvious next step, but also uneasy that something was off, so he asked for time.

qa.q: Which question helped Ujjwal decide, and what did he choose?
qa.a: He asked whether he would have said yes if the treasurer job had been the first request; the answer was no, so he kept his floor and declined the rest.

qa.q: How might Kishore see Ujjwal's answer?
qa.a: Kishore was probably disappointed, since Kishore was building up to the treasurer job, but nodded because Ujjwal was still helping with his floor.

passage: Tenzin, you've just signed a lease and the landlord is asking for favours already? Sit. Let your Binita Didi tell you about my first flat in Siliguri. I was twenty-four. The landlord, a very polite man, asked for six months' rent in advance. Six! I said no; I didn't have it. He sighed, looked sad and said, 'Of course, of course, too much. Then just three months?' And I felt it, that little tug. He had come down so much. Surely I should come up a bit? I almost said yes. Then I remembered something my aunt used to say: pretend it's the first thing they asked. If he had walked in and said 'three months advance', would I have agreed? No. One month was normal, and three would have emptied my savings. So I said, 'One month, like everyone else.' He grumbled, but he gave me the keys. Remember that, Tenzin. You can always refuse the step in front of you.

qa.q: How many months' rent did the landlord first ask for in advance?
qa.a: He first asked for six months' rent in advance.

qa.q: What did Binita Didi feel when the landlord came down to three months?
qa.a: She felt a little tug, as if he had come down so much that she should come up a bit, and she almost said yes.

qa.q: What question did Binita Didi use, and how could Tenzin use it now?
qa.a: She pretended it was the first thing asked and saw she wouldn't agree to three months; Tenzin can ask the same about the landlord's favours and still say no.

qa.q: How might the landlord have seen Binita's answer?
qa.a: He grumbled, probably disappointed that the big-then-small ask didn't work, but he accepted it and gave her the keys.
